raw_case_text:
A 34-year-old man with no history of pulmonary disease was diagnosed with CML in September 2019 and was treated with 100 mg of dasatinib for 13 months. Although the dose of dasatinib was reduced to 80 mg because of cytopenia, he achieved an early molecular response at 3 months and maintained a major molecular response.
He visited the emergency department in October 2020 with complaints of CTCAE grade 1 fever and grade 2 headache persisting for 1 week. On examination, he was normotensive but showed fever and tachycardia of 38.3 C and 103 beats per minute, respectively. His respiratory rate was 19 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation was 96% on room air. Physical examination results, including chest auscultation, were unremarkable. The WBC count was 4.05 x 103/microl, with 59.1% of segmented neutrophils. Except for elevations in grade 1 liver enzymes (aspartate transferase, 53 IU/L; alanine transferase, 51 IU/L) and mild elevation in CRP (1.52 mg/dl; reference range, 0-0.5 mg/dl), there were no significant abnormalities in other laboratory parameters. Chest radiography performed 1 week later showed no abnormalities. However, the fever persisted despite prescribing antipyretics; therefore, a chest CT scan was performed on the 11th day of fever. Chest CT findings revealed ill-defined GGO and consolidation, especially in the left lower lung field (shown in Figure 1(c)). Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid analysis showed a lymphocyte-dominant pattern with no evidence of infection, including pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP), cytomegalovirus (CMV), respiratory virus, tuberculosis, or fungus. Echocardiography performed to exclude cardiac problems did not reveal any significant abnormal findings. Because of a suspected diagnosis of dasatinib-associated interstitial pneumonitis, dasatinib was discontinued. The fever resolved 3 days after the discontinuation of dasatinib, and TKI therapy was resumed 16 days after the discontinuation of the TKI, changing to imatinib. Follow-up chest CT performed after 3 months showed a decreased extent of the previously noted GGO (shown in Figure 1(d)). With regular outpatient department visits, the patient maintained molecular response 4.0, without significant toxicity to imatinib.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 34-year-old man with chronic myeloid leukemia treated with dasatinib for 13 months presented to the emergency department in October 2020 with a 1-week history of CTCAE grade 1 fever and grade 2 headache.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed with chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) in September 2019, the patient had been treated with dasatinib (initially 100 mg/day, reduced to 80 mg/day for cytopenia) for 13 months, achieving and maintaining a major molecular response. In October 2020, he presented to the emergency department with 1 week of persistent fever and moderate headache unresponsive to antipyretics.
subjective.past_medical_history: Chronic myeloid leukemia (diagnosed September 2019) in major molecular response on dasatinib 80 mg/day; no prior pulmonary disease.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for persistent fever and headache for 11 days; negative for respiratory complaints. Home medication was dasatinib 80 mg/day.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vital signs: Normotensive, febrile at 38.3 °C, tachycardic at 103 beats/min, respiratory rate 19 breaths/min, and room-air SpO2 96%. Physical examination including chest auscultation was unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: WBC 4.05 x 10^3/μL (59.1% segmented neutrophils), mild grade 1 transaminitis (AST 53 IU/L, ALT 51 IU/L), and mildly elevated C-reactive protein (CRP 1.52 mg/dL, reference: 0–0.5 mg/dL). Imaging: Chest radiograph at 1 week of fever was normal; transthoracic echocardiography was normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT scan (performed on day 11 of persistent fever): Ill-defined ground-glass opacities (GGO) and consolidation, predominantly in the left lower lung field. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Lymphocyte-predominant cellular pattern with no evidence of infection, testing negative for Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP), cytomegalovirus (CMV), respiratory viruses, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and fungi.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Dasatinib-associated lymphocytic interstitial pneumonitis presenting as isolated fever and headache, confirmed by left lower lobe ground-glass opacity/consolidation on day 11 chest CT, lymphocyte-predominant BAL fluid with negative testing for Pneumocystis pneumonia, CMV, TB, viruses, and fungi, and rapid defervescence within 3 days of stopping dasatinib. Plan and clinical course: Dasatinib was discontinued, resolving the fever within 3 days; 16 days later, tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy was safely switched to imatinib, resulting in regression of left lower lobe GGOs on 3-month follow-up chest CT and sustained deep molecular response (MR 4.0).
